mean: to learn a fact or the truth, often by asking or checking
ex: Can you find out what time the last bus leaves Varanasi for Prayagraj on Sunday?
note: 'I came to know' is common in India; 'I found out' sounds more natural elsewhere. Say 'find out about it'.

mean: to stop trying, or to stop a habit
ex: Arjun refused to give up even after failing the CA final twice.
note: Separable: 'give it up', never 'give up it'. Use -ing after it: 'give up eating sugar'. 'Give up on someone' = stop hoping.

mean: to examine a problem or complaint to find out the facts
ex: The railway helpline promised to look into my complaint about the broken AC in coach B3.
note: Not separable: 'look into it', never 'look it into'. 'I'll look into it' is a polite office promise, so do follow it up.

mean: to make someone notice a fact, often a mistake
ex: Thanks for taking the time to point out the error in the GST figure before the invoice went out.
note: Separable: 'point it out'. A common pattern is 'point out that...'. Softer than 'correct': 'May I point out one thing?'

mean: to start talking about a subject
ex: Please don't bring up the property dispute at Nani's birthday lunch; everyone will start shouting.
note: Separable: 'bring it up'. Second meaning: to raise a child ('She was brought up in Patna').

mean: to continue doing something
ex: Sorry for the interruption, Professor Iyer; please carry on with the lecture.
note: Mostly spoken; in formal writing 'continue' is better. Use 'carry on + -ing' or 'carry on with + noun'.

mean: to find or meet by chance; also, to seem a certain way
ex: If you come across a good tailor in Lajpat Nagar, please send me the number.
note: Two meanings: find by chance ('come across an old letter') and seem ('He comes across as arrogant'). Not separable.

mean: to understand or solve something after thinking about it
ex: Priya spent the whole evening trying to figure out why the hostel Wi-Fi kept disconnecting.
note: Casual but fine at work. Separable: 'figure it out'. 'Work out' means the same and sounds more British.

mean: to delay doing something until later
ex: Stop trying to put off the dentist visit, Rahul; that tooth won't fix itself.
note: Separable: 'put it off'. Also means 'make someone dislike': 'His rudeness put me off.' 'Postpone' is the formal word.

mean: to say no to an offer, request or invitation
ex: It was hard to turn down a job in Dubai, but Faisal wanted to stay near his parents in Lucknow.
note: Separable: 'turn it down', never 'turn down it'. Also means lower the volume: 'turn the TV down'. 'Reject' sounds harsher.

mean: to decide that something is not possible or not the cause
ex: The doctor ordered a blood test to rule out dengue before treating the fever as viral.
note: Very common in news: 'Police have not ruled out foul play.' Separable: 'rule it out'.

mean: to support a claim with proof, or to support a person
ex: If you say sales fell because of the rains, back up the claim with numbers from each district.
note: Also means to copy computer data. The verb is two words (back up); the noun is one (a backup).

mean: to fix a problem or put things in order
ex: Let me sort out the seating plan before the baraat arrives.
note: Friendly and common in British and Indian speech. Separable: 'sort it out'. 'Sorted!' means everything is fixed.

mean: to start or arrange something, such as a business, meeting or system
ex: My cousin Joseph left his bank job to set up a cloud kitchen in Pune.
note: Verb: two words (set up). Noun: 'a setup' or 'a set-up'. 'Set someone up' can also mean trick them into looking guilty.

mean: to think of an idea, plan or answer
ex: The team has two days to come up with a cheaper design for the solar water pump.
note: Cannot be split: 'come up with it', never 'come it up with'. Use it for new ideas; 'devise' is the formal version.

mean: to finish what you started or promised
hi: बात पूरी करना, अंजाम तक पहुँचाना
ex: Many people announce a fitness plan on New Year's Day; few follow through after the first week.
note: Not 'follow up' (check again later): follow through = actually complete it. In cricket, the follow-through is the end of the bowling action.

mean: to make something seem less important or serious than it is
ex: The airline tried to play down the delay, but passengers had been stuck at Chennai airport for six hours.
note: Opposite: 'play up'. Separable: 'play it down'. Common in news: 'Officials played down fears of a shortage.' Also one word: 'downplay'.

mean: to refuse to take something seriously or to listen to it
ex: Don't brush off a chest pain as gas, Papa; get an ECG done today.
note: Separable: 'brush it off'. It hints at carelessness. 'Give someone the brush-off' = rudely reject them.

mean: to be as good as people expected
ex: The new biryani place in Hyderabad did not live up to the hype on Instagram.
note: Here 'live' rhymes with 'give', not 'five'. Cannot be split. Often negative: 'failed to live up to'.

mean: (of a plan or deal) to fail and not happen
hi: बात न बनना, खटाई में पड़ना
ex: Get the agreement in writing, or the flat deal may fall through at the last minute.
with: fall through at the last minute
note: Used for plans and deals, not people: 'The deal fell through.' It takes no object.

mean: to become popular; also, to finally understand
ex: Nobody expected UPI to catch on so fast among sabziwalas and chai stalls.
note: Two senses: become popular ('the trend caught on') and understand ('she caught on to the trick'). Casual but fine at work.

mean: to pass quickly over a problem so that people don't notice it
ex: The annual report seems to gloss over the losses in the Kolkata branch.
note: Always critical: it suggests hiding something. Not split in normal use: 'gloss over it'.

mean: to solve small problems or differences before things go ahead
ex: The two families met over chai to iron out the last details of the wedding budget.
note: Picture pressing creases flat. Used for small problems, not big crises. Separable: 'iron them out'. Say EYE-urn, not 'eye-RON'.

mean: to give your opinion in a discussion, often as an expert
ex: Before we finalise the leave policy, I'd like Meenakshi from legal to weigh in.
note: Fine at work and in news. Use 'on' + topic: 'weigh in on the debate'. Not separable.

mean: to think carefully about something for a while before deciding
ex: Take the weekend to mull over the offer from the Bengaluru startup before you reply.
instead: think about it for some time
note: Separable: 'mull it over'. It suggests slow, unhurried thinking.

mean: to stick to a choice even more firmly after people question it
ex: Instead of apologising, the anchor chose to double down on his claim in the next night's debate.
note: From card games (doubling a bet). American, now common in news. Usually critical (stubbornness), but can be positive: 'double down on quality'.

mean: to develop or end in a particular way
ex: Nobody knows how the Ranji season will pan out now that three key players are injured.
note: Casual. Often negative or uncertain: 'The plan didn't pan out.' From gold miners washing gravel in a pan.
